PulseChain bridge, governance and DeFi evidence audit
Evidence companion to the conditional mechanism report (main paper).
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 181

Research updated 29 September 2026. This paper reports public transaction observations, fixed-block
contract state and behavior identified in deployed source. Its conclusions concern the audited addresses
and stated search ranges. It does not attribute motives, legal character or human ownership to the
activity.
Findings
The recorded PulseChain history includes gateway-mediated ARB and GRT mints, standard-gateway
escrow releases, Aave governance executions and upgrades, Across ownership and implementation
changes, wrapper trades, Curve exchanges and Aave debt repayments. Each is an independently
evidenced observation. The collected records do not yet connect them into one reconciled source-
deposit, destination-issuance, purchase and settlement history.
The gateway census covers 129 token addresses appearing in the selected router's returned registration
logs and nine destination gateways. Their accounting differs: some transfer escrow, some invoke token-
specific issuance, and WETH wraps received native currency. The queried existing OUSD, eUSD, mUSD,
FRAX and three Aave V3 stable receipt addresses select the standard escrow gateway.
Reserve's copied eUSD deployment is version 2.0.0. Its fourteen registered token/plugin pairs and prime
basket match between the inherited snapshot and the audit endpoint. Its active basket contains four
lending receipts. Cached basket status, current plugin price reads and oracle timestamps are reported
separately; a successful present-day issuance has not been established by these getter calls.
Governance authority is investigated through roles and recorded changes, rather than inferred from
unrelated protocol control.
Earlier conditional mechanism studies remain separately identified among the companion studies.
Hypothetical balances, assumed governance ownership and local experiments are not evidence that
public-chain transactions occurred.
Scope and evidence method
“L1” means PulseChain, chain 369. “pARB” means a proposed execution network settling to its copied
Arbitrum contracts; it does not identify the operating Ethereum Arbitrum network. The prefix “p”
distinguishes copied assets from issuer-supported Ethereum balances. For readability, tables use familiar
token symbols, but all state and transaction findings concern PulseChain.
The PulseChain mainnet README identifies inherited Ethereum state through block 17,232,999, dated
10 May 2023 at 22:36:11 UTC. Historical searches start at 17,233,000. Copying Ethereum state copied
its L1 bridge and governance contracts; it did not by itself copy each rollup’s separate execution
database. Across is a bridge system, rather than an additional L2 execution database.
The principal endpoint is block 27,659,393, hash 
0xc5e582cd902f4bff3b1aa325b9b564fcd5d6dc0ffa77a03fcd105b65c6390275, on 28 September 2026. Research
completed on the following day still uses this fixed endpoint. Reads use https://rpc.pulsechain.com;
explorer data and published source supplement them. Cited historical events were reconciled with
successful receipts and block hashes. The two examined bridge transactions also have historical 
trace_transaction results. Otter’s examined trace pages were inaccessible to the research clients; the RPC
supplied the actual traces.
This is reproducible evidence from one RPC and related explorer services, not independently verified
consensus or source-chain state proofs. Negative event findings apply only to the selected addresses,
event signatures, range and provider completeness. An endpoint getter cannot exclude a temporary
historical change, and an event cannot establish a human operator’s identity.

What the two examined bridge transactions prove

corresponding zero-address Transfer, gateway withdrawal and outbox execution events.

The mint was 972,406,600,390,402,296,078,726,883,998.977902572465996426 ARB, using the
token’s 18 decimals. The total-supply difference between the preceding block and the execution block
exactly matches that amount. This is token units, not dollar value. Published implementations identify

This positively supports the destination-mint claim. The receipt and trace do not independently prove an
equal source balance was locked, that it remains locked, or that source redemption and destination
burning reconcile. The source-side runtime and escrow history have not been supplied or verified. A
further historical decode found that the ARB message’s recorded source-block and timestamp fields do
not describe a plausible source chronology. They therefore supply no independent evidence of a native
source deposit before or after the fork. The preceding rollup confirmation is only a temporal neighbor; a
direct message/root link was not established. This reinforces the distinction between the proved
destination mint and unproved source backing.

GRT: a second executed destination issuance
Transaction 0xf7ed5701… executed at block 27,434,949, on 1 September 2026 at 13:42:05 UTC.
The historical trace follows outbox → bridge → GRT gateway → GraphToken.mint → GraphToken.transferFrom. Its
successful receipt records a mint of 62,875,936.675361278837595998 GRT to escrow 
0x36aff7001294dae4c2ed4fdefc478a00de77f090. The total-supply change from the preceding block matches that
amount exactly. The trace reads 1 GRT already in escrow before minting; the escrow then transfers 
62,875,937.675361278837595998 GRT to 0xa0b347117a878da9942fa5c31b87c773a2969913. Thus the
delivered amount is the existing escrow contribution plus the minted shortfall.
The token is 0xc944e90c64b2c07662a292be6244bdf05cda44a7; its gateway is 
0x01cdc91b0a9ba741903aa3699bf4ce31d6c5cc06. At the endpoint the token's isMinter(gateway) returns true and the
gateway reports unpaused. The gateway's recorded cumulative mint allowance is 64,230,816.8555
GRT, and its recorded minted amount is 62,875,936.675361278837595998 GRT. Their difference is 
1,354,880.180138721162404002 GRT. The configured allowance accrual is 6.0365 GRT per block.
These are token-accounting quantities, not dollar values or a guarantee that a future transaction will
execute.
The allowance was configured before the fork, on 18 April 2023, with a zero allowance snapshot,
effective start block 17,018,986, and 6.0365 GRT per block. Historical getters at the inherited
boundary, transaction-predecessor block and transaction block agree on these parameters and the
gateway's minter permission. The selected configuration-event census contains no post-fork change. At
the mint block, accrued allowance was 62,875,960.6495 GRT; after this mint, 
23.974138721162404002 GRT remained. This is evidence of use of inherited, block-accrued capacity,
rather than evidence that someone increased the rate after the fork.

The GRT gateway returned two post-fork withdrawal events. The other is an 8 January 2025 escrow
release of 30,490,952.885900226731295138 GRT to 0xb8698cfffdaaf26ca21fe8aa560c18cc2b2f5996. Its
receipt contains no GRT mint. This identifies a recorded interaction with the previously discussed
address; it does not establish common ownership with the September transaction's parties.
The historical source design is L2 burn followed by L1 escrow release or shortfall minting. Official
pre-fork GIP-0037 introduced the minting allowance for L2-native indexing rewards, and the dated L2
gateway source calls bridgeBurn during withdrawal. It is not evidence that the same transferred GRT
remains locked in an L2 investment position. The GRT reconciliation study (Appendix 12) provides the
official proposal, pinned source, exact arithmetic and historical getter records. It does not claim
independently observed pARB source execution.
GRT uses its specialized mint permission and allowance accounting, whereas ARB uses its registered
reverse-token bridgeMint interface. Both destination mints are observed. Neither receipt independently
establishes source custody, source execution history or the human identity of the transaction sender.
What the broader transaction census adds
Combining the four escrow-family gateways, the GRT gateway and the five current or retired specialized
gateways produces 106 returned withdrawal events across 78 transactions and 91 token
addresses. All ten identified historical gateway addresses were queried over blocks 17,233,000–
27,659,393. ARB and GRT remain the two confirmed destination-mint cases within this selected history.
The selected gateway queries and recovered token-log partitions have no unresolved query gaps;
provider completeness and unqueried mechanisms remain separate limitations.
A separate post-fork search of the standard, custom, DAI and wstETH gateways returned 102
withdrawal events across 74 transactions and 90 token addresses. Their complete receipts
contain no zero-address ERC-20 Transfer. For 101 events, a same-token transfer exactly matches the
gateway amount and recipient; the remaining event's two outgoing transfers sum to the gateway's gross
amount. This screen identifies no additional mint candidate, but nonstandard issuance or rebasing
requires token-specific analysis rather than reliance on this event pattern alone. The receipt census
(Appendix 11) records methods, scope and the split-transfer reconciliation.
Historical router registration logs identify ten gateway addresses in total, including one retired LPT
gateway, compared with nine effective endpoint gateways. Current preferred routing alone also misses
actual withdrawals: GRT has a standard-gateway escrow transfer and LPT has a custom-gateway escrow
transfer in the returned history. Auditing only each token's current preferred gateway would omit those
transactions.
The LPT specialized gateway executed a withdrawal of 10,459,514.129760763228599483 LPT on 13
September 2024, in transaction 0x377c6bd1…. Its trace uses existing escrow, contains no external-
minter call, and its block-to-block total supply is unchanged. A mint branch exists in the gateway source,
but this transaction did not execute it. The specialized history (Appendix 20) records the separate ARB,
LPT, HGOLD, WETH and retired-gateway searches and their limits.

Evidentiary effect of GRT
The observed GRT shortfall mint establishes that insufficient L1 token escrow is not a universal bar to
destination issuance: a particular deployed gateway used its existing token-specific mint permission
to supply the shortfall. That result is stronger than merely locating a mint function in source code. It also
establishes that ARB is not the only observed destination mint model.
The conclusion remains token-specific. This transaction does not establish mint permission for the
existing DAI, USDC, USDT, eUSD, OUSD or Aave receipt contracts; it does not demonstrate continued
source investment; and it does not trace issued GRT into pDAI purchases or issuer collateral. Those are
distinct transaction and accounting questions. The main paper therefore records an executed bridge
issuance mechanism without treating it as a completed stablecoin funding or price-stabilization history.
Bridge and Portal accounting in inspected source
An ordinary L1-origin bridge escrows tokens on L1 and releases that inventory when an accepted return
message arrives. The MIM trace exemplifies release. A native-L2 reverse bridge can lock tokens on L2
and mint a destination representation through a specifically authorized L1 token. The ARB trace
establishes that destination leg, while source backing remains unverified. T oken-level burn/mint systems
form a third pattern: they require their own message validation and destination issuance permissions.
Aave Portal is separate application accounting. V3 mintUnbacked creates the reserve’s ordinary destination
aT oken and increases its unbacked balance. backUnbacked transfers actual destination underlying into that
reserve and reduces the outstanding amount. Source collateral can support a bridge’s obligation, but it
does not perform that destination transfer. This follows Aave’s BridgeLogic.
In underlying units, U_after = U_before + issuance − settlement. A purchased pDAI used for settlement
becomes reserve cash. It cannot simultaneously be counted as a separate bridge-escrow asset and free
treasury inventory. Similarly, a source vault receipt and the underlying it represents are one collateral
allocation, not two independent reserves.

The relevant vault standard is ERC-4626. Neither it nor ERC-20 mandates a bridge mint hook. A newly
issued representation also has a new identity unless it uses an already integrated token contract;
existing pools accept exact addresses.
Across: replenishing both sides without confusing delivery and minting
The May 2023 Across V2 model supports funding on both sides. User deposits replenish an origin
SpokePool; hub-to-spoke bridge transfers can replenish L2 inventory; L1 LP deposits and completed
spoke-to-hub returns can replenish L1 inventory. Fast fills use the relayer's existing destination tokens,
while validated bundles govern refunds and net rebalancing. These capabilities are present in the pinned
historical sources, rather than inferred from a modern Across version.
Consequently, a source deposit can remain in the L2 spoke while a recipient already has an L1 payment.
If a supported settlement pays the relayer on L2, the assets can stay on that network while ownership
moves to the relayer; they no longer remain in that spoke as the original deposit. Opposing flows and
pooled settlement can keep aggregate spoke balances replenished and reduce canonical bridge
transfers. The same units cannot be simultaneously counted as freely withdrawable by the depositor and
available to satisfy unrelated refunds.
These source-defined settlement operations do not themselves mint L1 stablecoins or LP shares against
arbitrary L2 deposits. One-direction L1 payouts still consume destination capital, which needs actual
replacement through incoming funds, offsets, bridge settlement or separately funded credit. Empty
canonical L1 escrow is not repaired solely by accumulating more source-side deposits. The Across
analysis (Appendix 7) contains a 100-unit balance example and the exact source references.
An L1 recipient can use delivered tokens in Aave or Curve, subject to the actual token, permissions and
local liquidity. The destination fill and DeFi action can be composed within one L1 transaction through a
suitable integration. The preceding L2 deposit and subsequent cross-chain settlement remain separate.

Thus L2 capital can support an L1 trade economically, while the actual trade spends destination capital.
A future source-chain refund cannot repay a flash loan that must settle before the destination
transaction ends.
The configured L1 spoke at 0x5c7bcd6e7de5423a257d81b442095a1a6ced35c5 has a verified inherited
implementation, 0xa667498f46457548f1d3ad557340b95fdb290148, that includes handleAcrossMessage and message-
bearing fill interfaces. Thus recipient callback capability was present in this proxy's fork baseline, rather
than merely available in a repository. A compatible receiver could use that callback for a funded
destination DeFi action. Inherited implementation source.
The configured proxy was upgraded on 30 June 2026, 04:52:25 UTC, at block 26,912,634, by 0xfeca…
d140, to 0x788e49c4e2b3414777d6671d7411951e81d35808. Its source is not explorer-verified, so the inherited source

They locally enabled issuance and executed small DAI mint/wrap/swap/settlement cycles. Another
destination-only experiment traversed eUSD → FRAX → USDC → DAI and left a settlement shortfall. These
were conditional execution demonstrations with modified local configuration, not public PulseChain
transactions and not verified source-L2 deposits. Their outputs and experiment identities are preserved;
they are excluded from this paper’s historical transaction trail. No such transaction experiments were
run for this retrospective update.

0.000000196841638655 DAI of Portal unbacked principal. A separate fixed-time experiment also left a

label are insufficient proof of a fully settled, profitable loop.

nominal 250-billion-input quotes did not show 250-billion payouts, and the local route did not establish

contract state and behavior identified in deployed source. Its conclusions concern the audited addresses
and stated search ranges. It does not attribute motives, legal character or human ownership to the

Findings
The recorded PulseChain history includes gateway-mediated ARB and GRT mints, standard-gateway
escrow releases, Aave governance executions and upgrades, Across ownership and implementation
changes, wrapper trades, Curve exchanges and Aave debt repayments. Each is an independently
evidenced observation. The collected records do not yet connect them into one reconciled source-
deposit, destination-issuance, purchase and settlement history.
The gateway census covers 129 token addresses appearing in the selected router's returned registration
logs and nine destination gateways. Their accounting differs: some transfer escrow, some invoke token-
specific issuance, and WETH wraps received native currency. The queried existing OUSD, eUSD, mUSD,
FRAX and three Aave V3 stable receipt addresses select the standard escrow gateway.
Reserve's copied eUSD deployment is version 2.0.0. Its fourteen registered token/plugin pairs and prime
basket match between the inherited snapshot and the audit endpoint. Its active basket contains four
lending receipts. Cached basket status, current plugin price reads and oracle timestamps are reported
separately; a successful present-day issuance has not been established by these getter calls.
Governance authority is investigated through roles and recorded changes, rather than inferred from
unrelated protocol control.
Earlier conditional mechanism studies remain separately identified among the companion studies.
Hypothetical balances, assumed governance ownership and local experiments are not evidence that
public-chain transactions occurred.
Scope and evidence method
“L1” means PulseChain, chain 369. “pARB” means a proposed execution network settling to its copied
Arbitrum contracts; it does not identify the operating Ethereum Arbitrum network. The prefix “p”
distinguishes copied assets from issuer-supported Ethereum balances. For readability, tables use familiar
token symbols, but all state and transaction findings concern PulseChain.
The PulseChain mainnet README identifies inherited Ethereum state through block 17,232,999, dated
10 May 2023 at 22:36:11 UTC. Historical searches start at 17,233,000. Copying Ethereum state copied
its L1 bridge and governance contracts; it did not by itself copy each rollup’s separate execution
database. Across is a bridge system, rather than an additional L2 execution database.
The principal endpoint is block 27,659,393, hash 
0xc5e582cd902f4bff3b1aa325b9b564fcd5d6dc0ffa77a03fcd105b65c6390275, on 28 September 2026. Research
completed on the following day still uses this fixed endpoint. Reads use https://rpc.pulsechain.com;

successful receipts and block hashes. The two examined bridge transactions also have historical

supplied the actual traces.
This is reproducible evidence from one RPC and related explorer services, not independently verified
consensus or source-chain state proofs. Negative event findings apply only to the selected addresses,

historical change, and an event cannot establish a human operator’s identity.

Evidentiary effect of GRT
The observed GRT shortfall mint establishes that insufficient L1 token escrow is not a universal bar to
destination issuance: a particular deployed gateway used its existing token-specific mint permission
to supply the shortfall. That result is stronger than merely locating a mint function in source code. It also
establishes that ARB is not the only observed destination mint model.
The conclusion remains token-specific. This transaction does not establish mint permission for the
existing DAI, USDC, USDT, eUSD, OUSD or Aave receipt contracts; it does not demonstrate continued
source investment; and it does not trace issued GRT into pDAI purchases or issuer collateral. Those are
distinct transaction and accounting questions. The main paper therefore records an executed bridge
issuance mechanism without treating it as a completed stablecoin funding or price-stabilization history.
Bridge and Portal accounting in inspected source
An ordinary L1-origin bridge escrows tokens on L1 and releases that inventory when an accepted return
message arrives. The MIM trace exemplifies release. A native-L2 reverse bridge can lock tokens on L2
and mint a destination representation through a specifically authorized L1 token. The ARB trace
establishes that destination leg, while source backing remains unverified. T oken-level burn/mint systems
form a third pattern: they require their own message validation and destination issuance permissions.
Aave Portal is separate application accounting. V3 mintUnbacked creates the reserve’s ordinary destination
aT oken and increases its unbacked balance. backUnbacked transfers actual destination underlying into that
reserve and reduces the outstanding amount. Source collateral can support a bridge’s obligation, but it
does not perform that destination transfer. This follows Aave’s BridgeLogic.
In underlying units, U_after = U_before + issuance − settlement. A purchased pDAI used for settlement
becomes reserve cash. It cannot simultaneously be counted as a separate bridge-escrow asset and free
treasury inventory. Similarly, a source vault receipt and the underlying it represents are one collateral
allocation, not two independent reserves.

The relevant vault standard is ERC-4626. Neither it nor ERC-20 mandates a bridge mint hook. A newly
issued representation also has a new identity unless it uses an already integrated token contract;
existing pools accept exact addresses.
Across: replenishing both sides without confusing delivery and minting
The May 2023 Across V2 model supports funding on both sides. User deposits replenish an origin
SpokePool; hub-to-spoke bridge transfers can replenish L2 inventory; L1 LP deposits and completed
spoke-to-hub returns can replenish L1 inventory. Fast fills use the relayer's existing destination tokens,
while validated bundles govern refunds and net rebalancing. These capabilities are present in the pinned
historical sources, rather than inferred from a modern Across version.
Consequently, a source deposit can remain in the L2 spoke while a recipient already has an L1 payment.
If a supported settlement pays the relayer on L2, the assets can stay on that network while ownership
moves to the relayer; they no longer remain in that spoke as the original deposit. Opposing flows and
pooled settlement can keep aggregate spoke balances replenished and reduce canonical bridge
transfers. The same units cannot be simultaneously counted as freely withdrawable by the depositor and
available to satisfy unrelated refunds.
These source-defined settlement operations do not themselves mint L1 stablecoins or LP shares against
arbitrary L2 deposits. One-direction L1 payouts still consume destination capital, which needs actual
replacement through incoming funds, offsets, bridge settlement or separately funded credit. Empty
canonical L1 escrow is not repaired solely by accumulating more source-side deposits. The Across
analysis (Appendix 7) contains a 100-unit balance example and the exact source references.
An L1 recipient can use delivered tokens in Aave or Curve, subject to the actual token, permissions and
local liquidity. The destination fill and DeFi action can be composed within one L1 transaction through a
suitable integration. The preceding L2 deposit and subsequent cross-chain settlement remain separate.
